Thought for 19m 16s

Yes. In fact, the asymptotic supremum is exactly 1+o(1). The upper bound follows from a random divisibility-chain argument; the quoted examples with Ω(n)=k show the constant 1 is sharp.

Let Ω(n) denote the number of prime factors of n, counted with multiplicity, and write pα∥n when pα∣n but pα+1∤n.

The random chain

For every prime p, let Yp be independent with exponential tail

P(Yp≥t)=p−t(t≥0).

Equivalently, Yp is exponential with rate log⁡p. For t>1, define

N(t):=∏pp⌊Yp/t⌋.

This is almost surely a finite integer for every t>1, because

∑pP(Yp≥t)=∑pp−t<∞.

Also, if t1>t2>1, then

⌊Yp/t1⌋≤⌊Yp/t2⌋

for every prime p, so

N(t1)∣N(t2).

Thus, as t decreases from ∞ to 1, the values N(t) form a random divisibility chain.

For an integer n≥2, define

Hn:={∃ t>1:N(t)=n},

and let

h(n):=P(Hn).

If A is primitive, then the events {Ha:a∈A} are pairwise disjoint: if a single chain hits both a and b, then one of a,b divides the other. Hence, for every primitive set A,

∑a∈Ah(a)≤1.

So it remains to show that, uniformly for large n,

h(n)≥(1−o(1))1nlog⁡n.

Exact hitting probability

Let

n=∏pα∥npα.

The chain hits n when, for some t>1, the required prime-power thresholds have appeared but no forbidden threshold has appeared. A direct calculation gives

h(n)=∫1∞n−tζ(t)(∑pα∥nαlog⁡p1−p−t) dt.

Here is the derivation. Suppose the last required threshold is the α-th threshold of a prime pα∥n, occurring at parameter t. Then Yp=αt, with density

αlog⁡p⋅p−αt dt.

For every other qβ∥n, we need

βt<Yq<(β+1)t,

which has probability

q−βt(1−q−t).

For every prime r∤n, we need Yr<t, which has probability 1−r−t. Multiplying and summing over the possible final primes gives

h(n)=∑pα∥n∫1∞αlog⁡p⋅p−αt∏qβ∥nq≠pq−βt(1−q−t)∏r∤n(1−r−t) dt=∫1∞n−tζ(t)(∑pα∥nαlog⁡p1−p−t) dt.

Now observe that for t>1,

∑pα∥nαlog⁡p1−p−t≥∑pα∥nαlog⁡p=log⁡n.

Therefore

h(n)≥(log⁡n)∫1∞n−tζ(t) dt.

Let L=log⁡n. Restricting the integral to 1<t<1+δ, with δ>0, and writing t=1+σ, we get

h(n)≥Ln−1∫0δe−Lσζ(1+σ) dσ.

Since

ζ(1+σ)=1σ+O(1)(σ↓0),

we have, uniformly for 0<σ≤δ,

1ζ(1+σ)≥(1−η(δ))σ,

where η(δ)→0 as δ→0. Hence

h(n)≥(1−η(δ))Ln−1∫0δe−Lσσ dσ=(1−η(δ))1nL(1−e−δL(1+δL)).

Choose, for example,

δ=δx:=(log⁡x)−1/2.

Then for every n≥x, L=log⁡n≥log⁡x, so

e−δxL(1+δxL)≤e−log⁡x(1+log⁡x)=o(1),

and also η(δx)=o(1). Thus, uniformly for all n≥x,

h(n)≥(1−o(1))1nlog⁡n.

Applying the chain to a primitive set

Let A⊂[x,∞) be primitive. For every finite B⊂A, the disjointness of the hitting events gives

∑b∈Bh(b)≤1.

Using the uniform lower bound for h(b), we obtain

(1−o(1))∑b∈B1blog⁡b≤∑b∈Bh(b)≤1.

Therefore

∑b∈B1blog⁡b≤1+o(1),

with the o(1) depending only on x, not on B or A. Taking the supremum over finite B⊂A gives

∑a∈A1alog⁡a≤1+o(1).

So the proposed assertion is true.

Moreover, the constant 1 is best possible: for Ak={n:Ω(n)=k}, one has Ak⊂[2k,∞), Ak is primitive, and your quoted asymptotic gives

∑Ω(n)=k1nlog⁡n=1−(c+o(1))k22−k.

Thus the asymptotic upper bound 1+o(1) cannot be replaced by anything below 1.
